clue.text: Marked on the surface, Puck going in to work …

indicators.note: the mischievous sprite is placed inside the word for work, as if entering it

parts.note: to ply a trade is to work at it
Puck is the mischievous sprite of A Midsummer Night's Dream, an imp; also a Guardian setter

explanation.surface: A setter called Puck sets to work, leaving something blemished, with the ellipsis carrying on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Puck, like many names in this puzzle, is a fellow Guardian crossword setter, but here he is just a sprite.
explanation.definitionFit: A face covered in spots or pustules is literally marked on its surface.

clue.text: Sticky stuff from Araucaria and Boatman?

parts.note: Araucaria is the genus of the monkey puzzle tree, a conifer; also the late great Guardian setter
a tar is a sailor; Boatman is also a Guardian setter

explanation.surface: Asking what gummy substance two Guardian crossword setters might produce.
explanation.walkthrough: Both names are Guardian setters, but here Araucaria is the tree genus it was named after and Boatman is a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: Pine tar is a viscous resin product used on baseball bats and ropes, a classic tacky substance.

clue.text: Dope finished study

parts.note: a dope is a fool, as is a mug
time is up when it is finished

explanation.surface: Drugs taken, someone has completed their research.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dope' suggests drugs; here it is a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: To mug up is British slang for cramming, learning a subject intensively before an exam.

clue.text: Philistine's top brought down?

parts.note: something brought down is set low
the brow is the top of the face, or of a hill

explanation.surface: Wondering whether an uncultured person's head was lowered.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for is, linking definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A philistine is someone without taste for art or culture, an uncultivated person of simple tastes.

clue.text: … back in business, like Crucible and Pan?

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter, here of business

parts.note: only its last letter is used
a crucible and a pan are both pots, so something like them is pot-like; potty is also a child's chamber pot

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue, two fellow setters, Crucible and Pan, are pictured as blemished and back at work.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition shares the ellipsis with the clue before: both answers mean marked with spots. Crucible and Pan are Guardian setters, but here they are just two kinds of pot.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer, like the previous one, means covered in pimples, blemished on the skin, which the ellipsis links to the earlier clue.

clue.text: Copied, Picaroon and Boatman?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a ... edition is an unauthorised copy, so the word works as an adjective for copied goods
second meaning: a picaroon is a sea rover, and a buccaneer is a seafaring boatman of sorts; both are also Guardian setters

explanation.surface: Accusing two Guardian setters of plagiarism.
explanation.walkthrough: Picaroon and Boatman are both Guardian setters, but the clue reads them literally: a plunderer and a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both an illegal duplicate, as in bootleg media, and a robber at sea.

clue.text: Confiscated by solicitor, contaminated doses thrown away

indicators.note: the rearranged doses are taken in by the solicitor, enclosed in that word

parts.note: a tout solicits custom, as a hawker does

indicators.note: contaminated doses are spoiled, so their letters are corrupted into a new order

parts.note: the word doses supplies the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A lawyer seizes some tainted medicine and disposes of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solicitor' suggests a British lawyer; here it is someone who solicits business, a tout.
explanation.definitionFit: Something discarded or ejected has been chucked out, the phrasal verb for getting rid of it.

clue.text: Housework coming up including cutting of wood — bore!

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: DIY, do-it-yourself, is work on your own house

indicators.note: a cutting of the word for wood is that word trimmed of its last letter

parts.note: elder is a tree, and its timber

explanation.surface: Someone finds DIY with woodwork tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'including' is the containment: the trimmed tree sits inside the reversed DIY. 'Bore' is a verb in the past, as in a tree bore fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A tree that bore fruit produced it, so bore and the answer are both past tenses of producing a crop.

clue.text: See 15
Make out number, second and third reversed

indicators.note: the second and third letters of the word for a number swap places

parts.note: a song is a musical number

explanation.surface: An instruction, apparently about a list of numbers, telling you to swap two items around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' looks like a figure but is a song in a show; its second and third letters change places.
explanation.definitionFit: To make out is informal for kissing passionately, which is the British slang term for a long kiss.

clue.text: Servers with perfect hair

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, written AI in crosswords as the digit 1 resembles the letter I
tresses are long locks of hair

explanation.surface: Restaurant staff admired for their flawless hairstyles.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 means excellent; the 1 is read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Women who bring food and drink to tables in a restaurant are servers by occupation.

clue.text: State of shock taking whippings from behind, rump finally bandaged up

indicators.note: the final letter is wrapped inside the other letters as a bandage would enclose it
the word for whippings is read starting from its back end

parts.note: routs are heavy defeats, whippings in the sporting sense

indicators.note: only the last letter of rump is used

parts.note: only its final letter is used

explanation.surface: A grim scene of corporal punishment leaving someone dazed, with a bandaged backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whippings' suggests beatings, but here it means sporting defeats; the beaten imagery is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: A stupor is a dazed condition of near-unconsciousness, such as follows a severe shock.

clue.text: Tramp in artist almost warmed up

indicators.note: the word for tramp sits inside the shortened artist
the artist's name loses its last letter

parts.note: Francisco Goya, the Spanish painter
to tramp is to tread heavily; Tramp is also a Guardian setter

explanation.surface: A vagrant sheltering inside a painter's house nearly gets warm.
explanation.definitionFit: Athletes who have warmed up have prepared themselves for the event to come.

clue.text: Literary squire we learnt foiled mutiny in the end

indicators.note: plans that are foiled are thrown into disarray, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: these words supply the letters to be rearranged

indicators.note: only the final letter of mutiny is taken

parts.note: only its final letter is used

explanation.surface: A squire in a novel discovers that the mutiny was eventually thwarted.
explanation.walkthrough: Squire Trelawney is a character in Stevenson's Treasure Island, a novel that does feature a mutiny.
explanation.definitionFit: Squire Trelawney finances the voyage in Robert Louis Stevenson's Treasure Island, a fictional landowner.

clue.text: FDR's agreement all needs to be sorted out before end of battle

indicators.note: the letters of all needs are put in a new order

parts.note: these words supply the letters to be rearranged

indicators.note: only the final letter of battle is taken

parts.note: only its final letter is used

explanation.surface: President Roosevelt's wartime deal had to tidy up every requirement before the fighting ended.
explanation.walkthrough: FDR is Franklin D Roosevelt, US president during the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: Lend-Lease was the 1941 US programme supplying Britain and its allies with materiel, a wartime arrangement.

clue.text: Seasonal tune: I acknowledge song's Bohemian

indicators.note: a bohemian lives unconventionally, so these letters are scattered into a free-spirited new order

parts.note: these words, apostrophe dropped, supply the seventeen letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone admitting that a Christmas carol's hero hails from Bohemia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bohemian' seems to name the carol's Duke of Bohemia, which fits the answer perfectly; it is the anagram signal. The apostrophe is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: This carol is sung every Christmas, which makes it a festive piece of music of the season.

clue.text: Function hosted by Boris in error

indicators.note: the answer is held within those words, as a guest is hosted

parts.note: the answer runs across borIS IN Error

explanation.surface: A political party thrown by Boris Johnson that should never have happened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Function' suggests a party, which fits the Boris Johnson lockdown scandal; here it is a trigonometric function.
explanation.definitionFit: Sine is a trigonometric function, the ratio of opposite side to hypotenuse in a right triangle.

clue.text: Shackled dog chained by Nutmeg, say

indicators.note: the dog is held within the other word as if tied up

parts.note: a nutmeg is the seed of a tropical tree; Nutmeg is also a Guardian setter
a cur is a mongrel dog

explanation.surface: A chained-up dog belonging to a setter called Nutmeg.
explanation.definitionFit: Something shackled is fastened tightly, made fast with chains or fetters.

clue.text: A jerk filling in hybrid puzzles

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the jerk fills the middle of the word for hybrid

parts.note: a cross is a hybrid of two breeds
a tic is an involuntary twitch

explanation.surface: An idiot completing a mixed set of puzzles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerk' looks like an insult for a person; here it is a twitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrostics are word puzzles in which initial letters of lines spell a hidden word.

clue.text: Old singer, if not plain beast?

parts.note: or means otherwise, if not
the bison roams the plains of North America

explanation.surface: Questioning whether a former singer was really just an ugly animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain' looks like unattractive; it is the prairie.
explanation.definitionFit: Roy Orbison was a 1960s American rock-and-roll vocalist, famous for Oh, Pretty Woman.

clue.text: Fashion dated, make better dresses

indicators.note: the outer word clothes the inner one, wrapped round it

parts.note: to cure is to heal
something dated is out of fashion, simply out

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned look is improved by better outfits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dresses' looks like clothes, matching the surface; it is the containment signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Couture is high-end designer clothing, the world of fashion houses.

clue.text: Notice Sphinx penning the ultimate in entertainment

indicators.note: the letter is enclosed, penned in, inside the other word

parts.note: the Sphinx set riddles, so it is a poser; Sphinx is also a Guardian setter

indicators.note: only the final letter of entertainment

parts.note: only its final letter is used

explanation.surface: A setter named Sphinx writes a review of a show.
explanation.definitionFit: A poster is a printed notice displayed in public, an advertisement on a wall.

clue.text: Seafood dish, name inspired by soaked bread

indicators.note: the name is breathed into the other word, held inside it

parts.note: sops are pieces of bread soaked in liquid
to call someone something is to name them

explanation.surface: A restaurant names a fish course after bread dipped in gravy.
explanation.definitionFit: Scallops are shellfish, a popular starter served pan-seared, a classic plate of shellfish.

clue.text: Boost Tramp and young Rover?

parts.note: a bum is a vagrant; Tramp is also a Guardian setter
Rover is a stock dog's name, and a young dog is a pup; Rover is also a Guardian setter

explanation.surface: Asking whether two Guardian setters, Tramp and Rover, could give something a lift.
explanation.walkthrough: Bum is American slang for a vagrant.
explanation.definitionFit: To bump up a price or rank is to raise it, increase it.

clue.text: Cheeseparer removing last of Roquefort from man

indicators.note: the letter is taken out of the word for man

parts.note: mister is a form of address for a man

indicators.note: only the final letter of Roquefort

parts.note: only its final letter is used

explanation.surface: A stingy person taking cheese away from someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheeseparer' and 'Roquefort' make the clue seem about cheese; a cheeseparer is a skinflint.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheeseparer is a stingy person who hoards money, someone extremely mean.

clue.text: English in Amsterdam working for the best crews

indicators.note: the letter for English goes inside the rearranged city name
the city's letters are put to work in a new order

parts.note: the city's name supplies the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An English worker in Amsterdam joins top teams.
explanation.definitionFit: Dream teams are the ideal line-ups, ensembles of the most talented members.

clue.text: Shed behind stable initially bolted

indicators.note: the shed is placed after the first letter
only the first letter of stable

parts.note: only its first letter is used
a hut is a small shed

explanation.surface: A horse bolted from a shed at the back of the stables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bolted' sounds like a horse running off, fitting the stable; it means locked with a bolt.
explanation.definitionFit: A door that is bolted is fastened, secured with a bar.

clue.text: Tedious Romeo in love

indicators.note: the letter for Romeo is placed within the word for love

parts.note: deary is an affectionate address like love
R is Romeo in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Romeo turns out to be boring when in love.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dull and gloomy is tiresome to experience.

clue.text: Small dish taking short butt and ash, for example

indicators.note: the word for butt is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: the end is the butt, the stub of a cigarette
ash is an example of a tree

explanation.surface: A tiny plate holding a cigarette end and its ash, like an ashtray.
explanation.walkthrough: Butt and ash conjure a smoker's ashtray; here they are a stub and a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrée in British usage is a modest course served before the main course.
